extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, advocates, applicants, and DHS adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and regulatory guidance for determining whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a "public charge" under DHS's final rule, including which public benefits are considered, how receipt is weighed, and procedural/attribution rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'primarily dependent'
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS considers the longstanding “primarily dependent” standard and treats the word “primarily” according to its ordinary meaning—namely main, chief, principal, of first importance, or foremost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS agrees recency and duration of benefit receipt should be considered when determining whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become primarily dependent on the government, but will not replace the ordinary meaning of 'primarily' with a numerical threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: No numerical threshold for 'primarily dependent'
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not define 'primarily dependent' in terms of a numerical threshold (e.g., cash assistance comprising 75–100% of income).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting a numerical threshold is unnecessary, could be arbitrary or inflexible, and would undermine individualized determinations contemplated by statute; the longstanding standard has never had a numerical threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public benefits considered (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS limits consideration, for public charge inadmissibility determinations, to: (1) public cash assistance for income maintenance and (2) long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach focuses on benefits most indicative of primary dependence and avoids considering the wide range of noncash supplemental programs that are not good predictors of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public cash assistance for income maintenance (included programs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public cash assistance for income maintenance includes SSI, TANF, and State, Tribal, territorial, or local cash benefit programs intended for income maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cash assistance is typically reserved for individuals with few other income sources and can allow reliance on government to the exclusion of independent income; DHS consulted benefit-granting agencies and finds cash assistance and long-term institutionalization best evidence of primary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-cash benefits generally excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Most non-cash benefits—such as CHIP, SNAP, Medicaid (other than Medicaid for long-term institutionalization at government expense), subsidized housing, and similar in-kind programs—are excluded from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many modern noncash programs are supplemental, provided to people who also have other income or employment, and therefore are not reliable indicators of primary dependence; excluding them avoids describing large portions of the population as 'public charges.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid and long-term institutionalization (narrow inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs that provide or cover the costs of long-term institutionalization at government expense (including Medicaid where it covers long-term institutionalization) are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS distinguishes HCBS (home- and community-based services), which do not pay for room and board and are excluded, from institutional long-term care which does provide 'total care for basic needs' and may indicate dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home- and community-based services (HCBS) excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: HCBS are excluded from public charge consideration because they do not provide 'total care for basic needs' (do not pay for room and board) and promote employment and community participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HHS emphasized the distinction in its letter to DHS; DHS excludes HCBS except to the extent they are coupled with receipt of cash assistance like SSI (receipt of which may be indicative of dependence).

rubrics_metrics.name: State/Tribal/territorial/local cash assistance treated like Federal cash assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider State, Tribal, territorial, and local cash assistance for income maintenance in public charge determinations and will not exclude such programs based solely on funding source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS is concerned about distinguishing programs that serve the same basic purpose solely by funding source; it will exclude special-purpose, supplemental, disaster and similar assistance but will consider general cash assistance across government levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special‑purpose, supplemental, disaster, and temporary assistance excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Special-purpose or supplemental programs (e.g., assistance restricted to particular uses), disaster assistance, similar emergency relief, and COVID-19 stimulus payments are not considered as cash assistance for income maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary or special-purpose aid does not indicate primary dependence; DHS explicitly will not consider COVID-19 treatments, preventive services, or stimulus payments and will not consider disaster assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax credits generally not considered (EITC, CTC)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider tax credits—such as the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) or the Child Tax Credit (CTC)—as public cash assistance for income maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: many moderate- or higher-income taxpayers qualify; difficulty distinguishing refundable portions; joint returns can make attribution to a noncitizen impossible; DHS also does not want to create fear/confusion about tax filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: General cash assistance vs. tax-credit‑style supports
rubrics_metrics.description: If a program functions like general cash assistance (unrestricted cash to families, not delivered via the tax system and not restricted in use), DHS would consider it cash assistance for income maintenance; if it is a restricted special-purpose payment or tax-credit delivered via tax returns, DHS would not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a future child allowance delivered as unrestricted cash (not a tax credit) would be considered unless classified as special-purpose; a tax-credit-delivered benefit like CTC would not be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency, duration, and amount of benefit receipt considered
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining likelihood of future primary dependence, DHS will consider not just the fact of receipt but also the recency, duration, and amount of public benefits received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are part of the totality-of-the-circumstances analysis and help distinguish short-term or minor assistance from sustained dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of a covered benefit is not dispositive (totality of circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Current or past receipt of SSI, TANF, or other covered public benefits is not alone dispositive of a finding that a noncitizen is likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will weigh benefit receipt along with other factors set out in new 8 CFR 212.22, including household income, assets, liabilities (exclusive of public benefits), and an Affidavit of Support under section 213A if required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution rules for benefits received on behalf of others (child-only benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not attribute receipt of cash assistance to a noncitizen if the noncitizen is receiving a public benefit solely on behalf of another (for example, TANF paid only on behalf of a child).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant is the child and subject to the public charge ground, DHS would consider the child's receipt; any such consideration is one factor among many and not outcome-determinative; recency, amount, and duration still apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small or short-term cash assistance unlikely to cause adverse determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Small amounts of cash assistance received for a limited period are unlikely, by themselves, to lead to an adverse public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes it would be unlikely to result in an adverse finding and that officers may request additional information about the program to determine whether a benefit should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants may supplement applications with explanations of temporary circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may include information explaining that benefit receipt was due to temporary circumstances (e.g., victimization, disaster) to assist officers in evaluating whether the benefits indicate likely future dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS did not add a categorical exemption for all victims of crime because existing exemptions may overlap and a blanket exclusion could ignore whether benefits were actually due to victimization; applicants should provide context where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS will provide a non-exclusive list in regulatory text and future guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS included a non-exclusive list of benefits not considered in the final regulatory text and intends to address benefit identification and related issues in future interpretative guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to clearly communicate to benefit administrators, recipients, and officers which benefits are not covered; DHS may further clarify which state/local programs are considered in guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of household income/assets/liabilities and Affidavit of Support
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's household income and assets, liabilities (exclusive of income received from public benefits or illegal activities), and any Affidavit of Support under section 213A as part of the totality of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are weighed along with benefit receipt (recency, amount, duration) and are important to assessing likelihood of future primary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed income programs generally not considered unless they operate as income maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Guaranteed income programs (local pilots between about $200–$1,000 monthly) would not be considered if they typically are not the primary source of income or are not means-tested; DHS would consider them if they function like cash assistance for income maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS recognizes variability across jurisdictions and will not treat guaranteed income as cash assistance for income maintenance unless it operates equivalently to such programs.
